source_read: PMC HTML full text PMC7682134 (title confirmed): Abstract, Background, Methods, Results with Tables 1 to 3 and footnotes, Discussion, Conclusion, declarations and the reference list (references 9, 13 and 22 checked) read in full. Fig. 1 (map of sites) not viewed.

claims.overstatement: No overstatement; the claim keeps association language, separates the coroners' background figures from the study's data and states the sampling limit. Two precision points: (1) 'Offered a short list of reasons ... the 314 most often chose ...' lists five reasons, but two of them (having no one to use with; not wanting to share or cheaper) were not offered options: they are themes the authors coded from free-text 'other' answers (Table 3, footnote a), so their shares are not comparable with the offered options and are probably undercounts; say so. (2) 'in 2019 more than half of illicit drug overdose deaths happened in a private residence': the paper says the place of injury was determined to be a private residence. 'Coroners' reports' is right: references 9 and 13 are British Columbia Coroners Service reports.
claims.note: All numbers found as printed. Recomputed: 314/414 = 75.8%, Wilson 95% CI 71.5% to 79.7% (same as the claim); 198/414 = 47.8%; 139/314 = 44.3% and 139/264 = 52.7%; 264 = 314 - 31 - 19; 44/314 = 14.0%; 37/314 = 11.8% (printed 11.7%); 30/314 = 9.6%; 27/314 = 8.6%. The 414 are the 486 who completed the survey less 37 missing and 35 prefer-not-to-say answers on using alone. 'Alone' is not defined in the question. The overdose item is an opioid or stimulant overdose in the past 6 months. No advice on amounts, timing or routes (the Background's public-health messages on amounts and pace are rightly not repeated).

anchors.extracted: 2018 Harm Reduction Client Survey, May to August 2018, 27 harm reduction supply distribution sites (37 approached, 10 declined for capacity); two-stage convenience sampling over a 2-week period per site; clients aged 19 or older, attending the sites, using illicit drugs in the previous 6 months, verbal consent; 10-minute survey, $5 CAD.

Single question on the percentage of time drugs were used alone in the last 7 days (0%, 1-25%, 26-50%, 51-75%, 76-100%, prefer not to say), dichotomized as any against none; 'alone' not defined; missing and prefer-not-to-say excluded.

anchors.locator: Results › Characteristics of participants who reported using drugs alone, 1st paragraph
anchors.extracted: 486 completed the survey; 37 missing and 35 prefer-not-to-say answers on the outcome excluded; analytic sample 414.

anchors.locator: Results › Characteristics of participants who reported using drugs alone, 3rd paragraph; Table 1
anchors.extracted: 314 of 414 (75.8%) used alone in the last 7 days; 198 (47.8%) more than 25% of the time. Used alone against not: no regular housing 37.6% against 24.0% (p < 0.01); opioid or stimulant overdose in the past 6 months 22.9% against 15.0% (p = 0.03); crack/cocaine 41.4% against 26.0% (p = 0.01); naloxone kit 67.8% against 66.0% (p = 0.61). Editors' Wilson 95% CI for 75.8%: 71.5% to 79.7%.

anchors.locator: Results › Factors associated with using drugs alone, 1st paragraph; Table 2 and footnote a
anchors.extracted: Final multivariable model on 306 observations: no regular housing AOR 2.27 (1.20-4.27), crack/cocaine 2.10 (1.15-3.82); not significant: opioids 1.59 (0.87-2.88), crystal meth 1.58 (0.86-2.88), opioid or stimulant overdose in past 6 months 1.71 (0.79-3.69, p = 0.17).

Those who used alone were asked for reasons with options: safer to be alone; more convenient and comfortable to use at home; don't want others to know; other (with free text); prefer not to say; more than one allowed.

anchors.locator: Results › Reasons for using drugs alone, 1st paragraph
anchors.extracted: 264 of 314 gave a reason (31 prefer not to say, 19 no response); 121 chose other and 113 wrote a reason; most were recoded to existing options; two new themes were created from free text (was alone or had no one to use with; do not want to share or cheaper); 19 could not be coded.

anchors.locator: Results › Reasons for using drugs alone, 2nd paragraph; Table 3
anchors.extracted: Of the 314: convenience and comfort 139 (44.3%); don't want others to know or stigma 44 (14.0%); was alone or no one to use with 37 (11.7%); safer alone 30 (9.6%); not wanting to share or cheaper 27 (8.6%); other 19 (6.1%); prefer not to say 31 (9.9%); no response 19 (6.1%). Stigma reason more frequent under 50 than at 50 or older (16.9% against 5.3%, p = 0.01); no other differences by gender or age.
Free-text answers included not having anyone to use with, not having access to an overdose prevention site, not being allowed to use in a transition home and severe pain.

British Columbia Coroners Service reports, not study data: in 2019 the place of injury was a private residence for over half of illicit drug overdose deaths and another residence for 26.5%; a September 2018 report of coroners' investigations found 69% of people who died of an overdose in 2016-2017 were using alone. No definitions of the deaths or of how using alone was established.

Self-reported data open to social-desirability bias; participants already connected to harm reduction services; findings may not generalize to all people who use substances in BC; people more affected by stigma may not attend.
Authors call using alone ubiquitous among people accessing harm reduction services and conclude that access to a safer supply of drugs is paramount, which the survey did not measure.

key_findings.correction: References 9 and 13 checked: both are British Columbia Coroners Service reports (2020 and 2018).
Reference 22 is Tsang, Papamihali, Crabtree and Buxton (2019), as the card says.

reporting_issues.note: Polysubstance use is absent from Table 2.
108 of 414 (26.1%) excluded from the model; no mention of clustering by site.

risk_of_bias.note: JBI prevalence, editors' summary moderate, agreed.

missed: Two of the five reported reasons (having no one to use with; not wanting to share or cheaper) exist only as themes coded from free-text 'other' answers, while the others were pre-printed options; the card records the recoding (key finding 7) but not that their percentages are not comparable with the offered options and are likely undercounts.
Age bands are labelled '> 50' in Tables 1 and 2 but described as 50 or older in the text (minor).
